Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes in seizure patterns before and after the treatment, as it relies on acute changes in brain activity. To aid in this analysis, we used electroencephalogram data collected from the surface of the brain during active seizures. From this data, we extracted features that represent the dynamic activity of the brain and used a supporting model to predict the likelihood of a seizure in the rest of the patient's recorded period. We focused on the part of the treated area of the brain that was heated to more than 40 degrees Celsius and analyzed how the probability of seizures in this region changed over time. This helped us assess the effectiveness of the treatment. To improve our evaluation, we used statistical methods to control for differences in patients and compare the treatment results to what might have been expected if the treated area of the brain didn't change. Using information from previous studies and our own, we found that an average patient's probability of a recurrence of seizures was reduced by more than half within the first month after the treatment, and reduced by over two-thirds within the first six months. This evidence strongly suggests that analyzing changes in the brain activity probability within the treated area can provide a supportive measure of the treatment's effectiveness and help determine the risk of a recurrence of seizures.
